claims.text: Standard rapid quenching of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produces an amorphous phase.
The rapidly quenched amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 retains high free volume.
The rapidly quenched alloy contains numerous nucleation sites for crystallization.
Ultrahigh cooling by optimized melt spinning can vitrify Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 more effectively than conventional rapid quenching.
A brief isothermal anneal just below Tg will improve amorphous retention in ultrahigh-cooled Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
A brief isothermal anneal just below Tg will improve the thermal stability of ultrahigh-cooled Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The sub-Tg anneal reduces free volume in the amorphous matrix.
The sub-Tg anneal relaxes internal stresses in the amorphous matrix.
Reducing free volume and internal stress decreases the density of crystallization nucleation sites.
Rapid quenching locks in a nonequilibrium amorphous structure rich in free volume and defects.
Excess free volume and defects make the rapidly quenched glass vulnerable to crystallization during reheating.
A sufficiently short sub-Tg anneal permits structural relaxation without nucleating crystalline phases.
The dual-stage protocol will raise the crystallization-onset temperature relative to standard rapid quenching.
The dual-stage protocol will reduce the crystallization rate during thermal analysis relative to standard rapid quenching.
The protocol requires an initial cooling rate fast enough to bypass crystallization.
An insufficient cooling rate can cause crystallization before the stabilizing anneal.
An excessively long or hot anneal can cause partial crystallization and negate the stabilization benefit.
